questions.text:
A graph shows the average monthly household water usage across New Zealand from 2014 to 2023, with a forecast extending to 2030. Key data points: 2014 ≈ 680 litres, 2018 ≈ 720 litres, 2023 = 750 litres, 2030 forecast = 900 litres. The trend shows gradual increase.

The forecast predicts NZ average monthly power use will increase from 750 litres (2023) to 900 litres (2030). Evaluate whether this forecast is valid. Support your evaluation with calculations and evidence.
questions.expectedAnswer: Forecast rate ~21.4 litres/year. Recent growth was ~6 litres/year (2018-2023), so forecast seems high...
questions.markingGuide: Valid evaluation should include: Forecast growth = (900 - 750) ÷ 7 = 21.4 litres/year. Compare with historical: 2014-2023 grew by 70 litres over 9 years ≈ 7.8 litres/year. The forecast rate is nearly 3× the historical rate — may be too optimistic. However, EV adoption and heat pump uptake could accelerate growth. COVID may have temporarily boosted home use. Achieved = describes trend. Merit = justifies with numerical evidence.

questions.text:
Two power companies offer different plans:

AquaSave Plans: $95/month (15,000 L), $130/month (25,000 L), $175/month (unlimited). Unused water credits carry over. Can share across household.

PureFlow Plans: $110/month (18,000 L), $145/month (30,000 L), $190/month (unlimited + free plumbing check). No carry-over. Cannot share.

Identify advantages and disadvantages of each provider's plans.
questions.expectedAnswer: AquaSave: cheaper unlimited, carry-over, can share. PureFlow: more litres per tier, annual check.
questions.markingGuide: AquaSave advantages: Cheaper entry and unlimited plans. Unused power carries over. Can share within household. Disadvantages: Lower litres allowances per tier. No extras. PureFlow advantages: Higher litres in mid-tier (500 vs 400). Free annual hot water check. Disadvantages: More expensive. No carry-over or sharing. Achieved = one advantage from each. Merit = two advantages each. Excellence = comprehensive comparison.

questions.text:
The Tupou family is moving to NZ from Samoa. There are two parents and three children. In Tonga they used about 20,000 L/month. They want a plan that covers their usage and allows garden irrigation.

Recommend either a AquaSave or PureFlow plan. Provide clear reasoning. State any assumptions.
questions.expectedAnswer: PureFlow $175 plan (500 litres) suits their usage. Or AquaSave unlimited if usage may increase.
questions.markingGuide: Consider: 500 litres usage. Family of 5. Moving from Samoa — may need time to adjust to NZ climate (more heating). PureFlow $175: 500 litres matches current usage exactly. AquaSave $160: only 400 litres (not enough). AquaSave unlimited $210 gives buffer. Assumptions: Usage may increase in NZ (colder climate). Family is in one household. Budget considerations. Achieved = recommendation with one reason. Merit = reasoning on usage AND cost. Excellence = comprehensive with assumptions.

questions.text:
A scatter plot shows the relationship between weekly grocery cost ($ per week, x-axis) and weekly exercise hours (minutes, y-axis) for different NZ suburbs. The plot shows a moderate negative trend — suburbs with higher grocery spending tend to have more exercise hours. Some expensive suburbs show a wide range of commute times.

A claim is made that 'paying more spending more on groceries means more exercise.' Evaluate this claim using the data.
questions.expectedAnswer: Moderate negative trend — higher rent doesn't guarantee short commute due to wide spread
questions.markingGuide: The scatter plot shows a moderate negative trend — suburbs with higher rents tend to have shorter commutes. This partially supports the claim. However, there is wide vertical spread at each rent level. Other factors (transport options, work location) also matter. Correlation doesn't prove causation. Achieved = uses negative trend. Merit = describes strength and discusses limitations.

questions.text:
Data shows average weekly grocery spending across NZ regions in 2023. Key data: NZ average = $210/week. Auckland is highest at $280. Gisborne is lowest at $145. The top 3 regions have a gap of $80 between them.

Compare features of the NZ rent data. Discuss at least TWO features.
questions.expectedAnswer: Large range ($330), mean ($210) pulled up by Auckland, right-skewed distribution
questions.markingGuide: Features: Range is large (650 - 320 = $330/week). Auckland ($650) is an outlier — pulls the mean up. Distribution is right-skewed (most regions below the average). The top 3 regions (Auckland, Wellington, Queenstown) are spread apart. Achieved = one feature. Merit = two features with evidence.

questions.text:
Comparison data for NZ and Australia:

Population: NZ ~5.1M, Australia ~26M
Gym membership rate: NZ 64.5%, Australia 66%
Average weekly groceries: NZ $210, Australia $240
Grocery increase 2020-2023: NZ +18%, Australia +12%
Proportion buying organic: NZ 35.5%, Australia 34%

NZ has faster-rising grocery costs than Australia. Using the data, identify and explain factors that could account for this. Support with numerical evidence.
questions.expectedAnswer: Similar ownership rates but NZ rents rose faster (18% vs 12%). Smaller population but similar rental proportion.
questions.markingGuide: Key factors: (1) NZ rents rose 18% vs Australia's 12% despite similar homeownership rates (64.5% vs 66%). (2) NZ has 5.1M people vs 26M — smaller market may be more volatile. (3) Similar proportions renting (35.5% vs 34%) but NZ may have tighter housing supply relative to demand. Achieved = one factor. Merit = one factor with numbers. Excellence = two+ factors with evidence.
